subject: History
name: History, Levels 9 and 10
syllabus: Victorian Curriculum F-10 Version 2.0: History, Levels 9 and 10

chapters.title: The making of the modern world, 1750 to 1918

points.title: Causes of the Industrial Revolution
points.brief: Industry took off in Britain from about 1750 because it had coal and iron, money to invest, colonies for markets and inventions such as the improved steam engine.

points.title: Effects of the Industrial Revolution
points.brief: Factories drew people into crowded cities with long hours, child labour and disease, which led to new laws on working conditions and to trade unions.

points.title: The movement of peoples
points.brief: Between 1750 and 1900 millions moved across the world, some by choice as free settlers and others by force as enslaved Africans or transported convicts.

points.title: European imperialism
points.brief: European powers took colonies across Asia, Africa and the Pacific for raw materials, markets and prestige, often by force and at great cost to local peoples.

points.title: New political ideas
points.brief: Ideas of individual rights, democracy, nationalism and socialism spread after the American and French revolutions and changed how people thought they should be governed.

points.title: The United Nations
points.brief: The United Nations was founded in 1945, after World War II, to keep peace between countries and promote human rights and cooperation.

points.title: The Cold War
points.brief: From 1945 to 1991 the United States and the Soviet Union competed for power through an arms race, a space race and wars fought by others, without fighting each other directly.

points.title: Decolonisation
points.brief: After 1945 most colonies in Asia and Africa won independence, some through negotiation and others through long wars, as with India in 1947 and Indonesia in 1949.

points.title: Movements for rights since 1945
points.brief: Civil rights, Indigenous rights, women's rights, LGBTQI+ rights and environmental movements used protest, courts and elections to change laws and attitudes.

points.title: The women's movement in Australia
points.brief: Australian women won the federal vote in 1902, equal pay rulings in 1969 and 1972, and the Sex Discrimination Act in 1984, changing their role in work and public life.

points.title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander societies in 1788
points.brief: In 1788 hundreds of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander nations, with their own languages, laws and ways of caring for Country, lived across the continent and islands.

points.title: Why Britain set up colonies
points.brief: Britain sent the First Fleet in 1788 to ease crowded prisons after losing its American colonies, and to gain a base in the Pacific, claiming land that was already owned.

points.title: Frontier conflict and resistance
points.brief: As settlers spread across Country, Aboriginal Peoples resisted in conflicts now called the Frontier Wars, such as the Eumeralla Wars on Gunditjmara Country in western Victoria.

points.title: The gold rushes
points.brief: Gold found in Victoria in 1851 brought hundreds of thousands of migrants, including from China, and miners' anger over licences led to the Eureka Stockade in 1854.

points.title: Federation
points.brief: On 1 January 1901 the six colonies joined to form the Commonwealth of Australia, and one of the new parliament's first laws was the Immigration Restriction Act behind the White Australia policy.

points.title: Australia as a social laboratory
points.brief: Early Australia tried new ideas such as the secret ballot, votes for women, a basic wage set in the Harvester case of 1907 and the age pension, though Aboriginal people were mostly left out.

points.title: Causes of World War I
points.brief: Militarism, alliances, imperial rivalry and nationalism set the stage, and the killing of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in 1914 set off the war.

points.title: Why Australians enlisted
points.brief: Australians joined up out of loyalty to Britain, adventure, pay and pressure from family and friends, and some Aboriginal men enlisted despite rules meant to keep them out.

points.title: Gallipoli
points.brief: Australian and New Zealand troops landed at Gallipoli on 25 April 1915 in a failed campaign against the Ottoman Empire and left in December after heavy losses.

points.title: The Western Front
points.brief: On the Western Front in France and Belgium, Australians fought trench battles such as Fromelles and Pozières in 1916, where machine guns and artillery caused huge losses.

points.title: The home front and conscription
points.brief: The war divided Australians at home, and two referendums in 1916 and 1917 on forcing men to serve overseas were both defeated.

points.title: The Anzac legend
points.brief: The Anzac legend praises courage and mateship, and historians debate how well it fits what soldiers lived through and whose stories it leaves out.

points.title: Causes of World War II
points.brief: The harsh Treaty of Versailles, the Great Depression and the expansion of Nazi Germany, Italy and Japan led to war in Europe in 1939 and the Pacific in 1941.

points.title: Australians in the Pacific war
points.brief: After Singapore fell in 1942, thousands of Australians became prisoners of war, and Australian troops fought back the Japanese advance on the Kokoda Track.

points.title: The home front in World War II
points.brief: Darwin was bombed in 1942, goods were rationed, women took on jobs men had done, and some people of enemy background were interned.

points.title: How warfare changed
points.brief: Between the wars, fighting moved from trenches to tanks, aircraft and aircraft carriers, whole societies were turned to the war effort, and atomic bombs ended World War II.

points.title: Causes of the Holocaust
points.brief: Long-held antisemitism, Nazi race ideas and laws such as the Nuremberg Laws of 1935 stripped Jewish people of their rights in Germany step by step.

points.title: Events of the Holocaust
points.brief: Persecution grew from Kristallnacht in 1938 to ghettos and then death camps such as Auschwitz, where the Nazis murdered about six million Jews and many others.

points.title: Experiences and perspectives in the Holocaust
points.brief: Historians study the Holocaust through the victims, the perpetrators, bystanders and those who resisted or rescued, and why people acted as they did.

points.title: Qing China and the West
points.brief: In the 1700s Qing China was rich and powerful and limited European trade to the port of Canton, seeing little it needed from the West.

points.title: The Opium Wars
points.brief: Britain won two Opium Wars from 1839 to keep selling opium in China, and the unequal treaties that followed gave away Hong Kong and opened Chinese ports.

points.title: The fall of the Qing
points.brief: Foreign pressure and revolts weakened the Qing, and the 1911 revolution ended over 2,000 years of rule by emperors and set up a republic.

points.title: Communist China
points.brief: Mao Zedong's Communist Party won the civil war in 1949, and campaigns such as the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution caused great suffering before market reforms began in 1978.

points.title: The opening of Japan
points.brief: American warships under Commodore Perry arrived in 1853 and forced Japan to open its ports to trade, ending two centuries of near isolation.

points.title: The Meiji Restoration
points.brief: From 1868 the Meiji government put the emperor back at the centre and rapidly built railways, factories, schools and a modern army on Western models.

points.title: Japan's expansion
points.brief: Japan defeated China and then Russia, took Korea in 1910 and invaded Manchuria in 1931, building an empire that led it into World War II.

points.title: Postwar Japan
points.brief: After defeat in 1945 Japan was occupied by the Allies, gained a new democratic constitution that gave up war, and grew into one of the world's largest economies.

units.title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander rights and freedoms

points.title: Protection laws and reserves
points.brief: From the mid-1800s colonial laws moved many Aboriginal people onto reserves and missions and let officials control where they lived, worked and married.

points.title: Coranderrk
points.brief: At Coranderrk near Healesville, Wurundjeri leader William Barak and his community farmed successfully and petitioned the government to keep their land.

points.title: The Day of Mourning
points.brief: On 26 January 1938, the 150th anniversary of British arrival, Aboriginal activists including William Cooper's Australian Aborigines' League held a Day of Mourning to demand equal rights.

points.title: The Freedom Ride
points.brief: In 1965 Charles Perkins led university students on a bus tour of country New South Wales to expose segregation at pools, cinemas and shops.

points.title: The Wave Hill walk-off
points.brief: In 1966 Vincent Lingiari led Gurindji workers off Wave Hill station over pay and conditions, and their strike became a fight for land that was returned in 1975.

points.title: The 1967 referendum
points.brief: Over 90 per cent of voters agreed to count Aboriginal people in the census and let the Commonwealth make laws for them, though it did not give the federal vote, which a 1962 law had already given.

points.title: Land rights and the Mabo decision
points.brief: In 1992 the High Court, in a case led by Eddie Koiki Mabo of the Meriam people, rejected terra nullius and recognised native title, followed by the Native Title Act in 1993.

points.title: The Stolen Generations and the Apology
points.brief: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children were forcibly removed from their families for decades, as the 1997 Bringing Them Home report found, and the nation apologised in 2008.

units.title: The globalising world, 1945 to the present

points.title: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
points.brief: Adopted by the United Nations in 1948, the declaration set out rights for every person, and Australia helped draft it while H. V. Evatt led the General Assembly.

points.title: Technology and living standards
points.brief: After 1945, cars, televisions, home appliances and later computers changed how people worked, shopped and spent their free time in countries like Australia.

points.title: Health and longer lives
points.brief: Antibiotics, vaccines such as the polio vaccine and better public health helped people live much longer in the 20th century.

points.title: Populate or perish
points.brief: After World War II Australia started a large migration program to grow its population and workforce, taking in displaced people from Europe and assisted British migrants.

points.title: Life for postwar migrants
points.brief: Many new arrivals stayed first in camps such as Bonegilla in Victoria and worked on projects like the Snowy Mountains Scheme, often facing hard conditions and prejudice.

points.title: The end of White Australia
points.brief: Governments removed race from immigration rules step by step until 1973, and Australia moved towards a policy of multiculturalism.

points.title: Refugees from Vietnam
points.brief: After the Vietnam War ended in 1975, many Vietnamese refugees came to Australia, some by boat, and their arrival tested and changed Australian attitudes.

points.title: The rise of environmental concern
points.brief: Rachel Carson's book Silent Spring in 1962 warned of pesticide harm, and growing worry about pollution led to the first Earth Day in 1970 and new environment groups.

points.title: Campaigns to save Tasmanian rivers
points.brief: The flooding of Lake Pedder in 1972 spurred activists, and the Franklin Dam blockade and a 1983 High Court ruling stopped a dam on the Franklin River.

points.title: Green bans
points.brief: In the 1970s builders' unions in Sydney refused to work on projects that would destroy bushland and historic buildings, joining workers and residents to protect places.

points.title: Climate change as a global issue
points.brief: From the 1980s scientists warned of global warming, and agreements such as the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement tried to get countries to cut emissions.

chapters.title: Analysing and arguing about the past

points.title: Evaluating sources as evidence
points.brief: Judging a source means asking who made it, why, when and for whom, and whether other sources back it up, before using it as evidence.

points.title: Perspectives and interpretations
points.brief: A perspective is how a person saw events at the time. An interpretation is a historian's later explanation, and historians can disagree about the same events.

points.title: Short-term and long-term causes
points.brief: Long-term causes build up over years, short-term causes or triggers spark an event, and consequences can be intended or unintended.

points.title: Judging historical significance
points.brief: Historians judge significance by how many people an event affected, how deeply, for how long and what it explains about today.

points.title: Writing a historical argument
points.brief: A historical argument states a clear contention, supports it with evidence from sources, deals with other views and cites its sources.
